title: Nature's extremes.
lede: Twenty-two of nature's record-holders, from the blue whale to a frog the size of a fingernail: what holds each record, and by how much.

card.title: Nature's extremes
card.desc: Twenty-two record-holders: the biggest, fastest, loudest, longest-lived and deadliest.

extras.title: Top Trumps: Nature's Extremes
extras.desc: A pack of record-holder cards. Play the computer, pick your best stat, and learn what beats what.

groups.label: Giants and minis
groups.note: The biggest, the tallest, the longest and the smallest.

groups.label: Speed, distance and depth
groups.note: Faster, further, higher and deeper than anything else.

groups.label: Senses and weapons
groups.note: The loudest, the strongest bite, and the most eyes.

groups.label: Life and death
groups.note: The longest lives, the shortest, and the deadliest.

items.figure: Up to about 30 m long and around 150 tonnes
items.hook: The largest animal that has ever lived, dinosaurs included: its heart is the size of a small car.

items.figure: One fungus in Oregon covers about 9.6 km²
items.hook: Mostly hidden underground as black bootlace-like threads; the honey-coloured mushrooms are just the tip.

items.figure: A quaking aspen colony in Utah: one root system, about 47,000 stems, roughly 6,000 tonnes
items.hook: Latin pando, 'I spread': what looks like a forest is a single tree.

items.figure: 62.4 cm with its legs stretched out
items.hook: Found in Guangxi, China, in 2014: longer than your arm.

items.figure: About 7 mm: it sits on a fingernail
items.hook: Brachycephalus pulex; pulex means flea. A 2024 study confirmed it smaller than the old record-holder, Paedophryne amauensis of Papua New Guinea (about 7.7 mm).

items.figure: A coast redwood, about 116 m tall
items.hook: Named after a Titan; its spot in Redwood National Park, California, is kept secret.

items.figure: Over 320 km/h (200 mph) in a dive
items.hook: It drops on its prey from above, folding its wings into a teardrop.

items.figure: About 100 to 120 km/h, in short bursts
items.hook: 0 to 60 mph in around three seconds, like a sports car, but only for a few hundred metres.

items.figure: Pole to pole and back: 70,000 km or more a year
items.hook: Chasing two summers a year, it sees more daylight than any other animal.

items.figure: Nearly 3,000 m down, and over three hours on one breath
11,300 m: one hit a plane over Ivory Coast in 1973
items.hook: Cruising altitude for a jet airliner.

items.figure: Clicks of around 230 decibels
items.hook: It hunts by sonar: the clicks echo back off squid in the dark.

items.figure: About 16,000 newtons (3,700 psi), measured
About 27 cm across: the size of a football
items.hook: Big eyes for spotting sperm whales (see: loudest animal) in the deep.

items.figure: Up to 200 tiny eyes round the edge of its shell
items.hook: The usual quiz answer; chitons, a kind of mollusc, can have even more.

items.figure: About 22 months
items.hook: Among mammals: the frilled shark and the Alpine salamander carry their young for years.

items.figure: A Seychelles giant tortoise, about 194 years old in 2026
items.hook: Hatched around 1832; he lives on St Helena, in the governor's garden.

items.figure: At least 272 years, perhaps nearly 400
items.hook: It grows about 1 cm a year and isn't grown up until it's around 150.

items.figure: As an adult, from minutes to a day or so
items.hook: Its group name, Ephemeroptera, gives us 'ephemeral'.

items.figure: Survives boiling, near absolute zero, radiation and the vacuum of space
items.hook: Also called the water bear or moss piglet; about half a millimetre long.

items.figure: Its sting can kill a person within minutes
Hundreds of thousands of deaths a year, mostly from malaria
